Sequence-based prediction of N6-methyladenosine (m6A) sites using a random forest model

m6APrediction predicts whether a candidate RNA site carries an N6-methyladenosine (m6A) modification, using only information that can be read off the transcript sequence and annotation: GC content, RNA type, RNA region, exon length, distance to the nearest exon junction, evolutionary conservation of the 5-mer context, and the DNA 5-mer itself.

The package is the deliverable of the BIO215 bioinformatics project. It packages the random forest model developed in Practical 4 and the prediction functions written in Practical 5 into a documented, installable R package, so that the same model can be reused from any R session instead of living inside a single Shiny app.

Why a sequence-based m6A predictor is useful

m6A is the most abundant internal modification of eukaryotic mRNA. It is deposited by the METTL3–METTL14 writer complex, recognised by reader proteins such as YTHDF1–3, and influences transcript stability, splicing and translation. Mapping m6A experimentally (MeRIP-seq, miCLIP, GLORIP) is expensive, needs large amounts of RNA, and gives antibody-dependent, region-level resolution.

Because the modification is enriched in a DRACH-type motif and correlates strongly with local sequence composition, exon architecture and evolutionary conservation, a model trained on those features can rank candidate sites before any wet-lab work. That is what this package provides: a fast, interpretable scoring function that turns a feature table — or a single 5-mer context — into a probability and a Positive/Negative call.

Installation

The package is hosted on GitHub. Install it with devtools (or remotes if you prefer a lighter dependency):

# install.packages("devtools")
devtools::install_github("Zzty2026/m6APrediction")

# or, without devtools
# install.packages("remotes")
remotes::install_github("Zzty2026/m6APrediction")

The package requires R (>= 3.5.0) and imports randomForest and stats. The fitted model (about 15 MB) and a 100-row example feature table are bundled with the package, so no external download is needed.

Quick start

library(m6APrediction)

# 1. Load the bundled model and example feature table
ml_fit <- readRDS(system.file("extdata", "rf_fit.rds",
                              package = "m6APrediction"))
example_df <- read.csv(system.file("extdata", "m6A_input_example.csv",
                                   package = "m6APrediction"))

# 2. Score many candidate sites at once
res <- prediction_multiple(ml_fit, example_df[1:5, ],
                           positive_threshold = 0.6)
res[, c("DNA_5mer", "predicted_m6A_prob", "predicted_m6A_status")]
#>   DNA_5mer predicted_m6A_prob predicted_m6A_status
#> 1    GAACA              0.876             Positive
#> 2    GAACC              0.000             Negative
#> 3    AAACT              0.498             Negative
#> ...

# 3. Score one site without building a data.frame
prediction_single(ml_fit,
                  gc_content = 0.6, RNA_type = "mRNA", RNA_region = "CDS",
                  exon_length = 12, distance_to_junction = 5,
                  evolutionary_conservation = 0.8, DNA_5mer = "GGACA")
#>  predicted_m6A_prob predicted_m6A_status
#>               "0.51"            "Positive"

Note that exon_length and distance_to_junction are expected already log2-transformed, and that DNA_5mer must be a five-nucleotide context with a central adenine (e.g. GGACA). The returned status is "Positive" only when the probability is strictly greater than the threshold; a probability equal to the threshold counts as "Negative".

Functions

Function Exported Purpose
prediction_multiple(ml_fit, feature_df, positive_threshold = 0.5) yes Score a table of candidate sites; returns the input columns plus predicted_m6A_prob and predicted_m6A_status.
prediction_single(ml_fit, gc_content, RNA_type, RNA_region, exon_length, distance_to_junction, evolutionary_conservation, DNA_5mer, positive_threshold = 0.5) yes Score one site from individual feature values; returns a named character vector.
dna_encoding(dna_strings) no (internal) Expand 5-mer strings into five positional nucleotide factors (nt_pos1–nt_pos5) on the fixed levels A, T, C, G.

Full help pages are available in R, e.g. ?prediction_multiple, ?prediction_single and ?dna_encoding.

Model performance

Performance of the random forest model, computed from the out-of-bag (OOB) votes of the fitted forest — i.e. predictions for each site made by the trees that did not see it during training, which is equivalent to a held-out evaluation:

ROC curve

Receiver operating characteristic curve of the m6A random forest model

Precision–recall curve

Precision-recall curve of the m6A random forest model

The ROC curve stays well above the diagonal and the precision–recall curve remains high across the recall range, which is the more informative view for this problem: m6A sites are a minority class, so a high overall accuracy would be misleading, whereas precision at high recall is what matters when the model is used to prioritise sites for experimental validation.

Reported performance: AUC = 0.89; PRC-AUC = 0.70 (4,805 negatives vs 11,248 positives in the training votes; the minority class is the positives, which is why PRC rather than ROC is the headline metric).

Reproducibility

devtools::document()          # regenerate NAMESPACE and man/*.Rd
devtools::load_all()          # load the development version
devtools::check(args = "--no-manual")   # full package check

devtools::check() runs both worked examples from the help pages. The examples load the bundled model themselves, so they also run in a fresh R session after installation.

Data

m6A_input_example.csv contains 100 candidate sites and the seven features used by the model. It is an illustrative table for demonstrating and testing the functions, not an independent test set, so it must not be used to estimate prediction accuracy.
